formulas.name: Accretion / dilution
formulas.note: Tamar all-stock: 1.252 ÷ 1.20 − 1 = +4.3 %. Positive is accretive, negative dilutive — and neither says anything about value.

formulas.name: New shares issued
formulas.note: All-stock: £500m ÷ £18 = 27.78m. The 50/50 deal issues half that: £250m ÷ £18 = 13.89m.

formulas.name: After-tax cost of debt (and cash)
formulas.note: New debt at 6 %: 4.5 % after tax. Cash works the same way on the interest you stop earning: 4 % becomes 3.0 %.

formulas.name: Cost of stock as a currency
formulas.note: Tamar at 15× pays 6.67 % when it pays in shares. Wychwood earns 8.0 % on the £500m offer — which is why the all-stock deal is accretive.

formulas.name: Goodwill
formulas.note: Wychwood: 500 − (220 book + 60 write-up) = £220m. A deferred-tax liability on the write-up shrinks the identifiable assets, so goodwill rises to £235m.

formulas.name: The deal test
formulas.note: Tamar: ≈ £167m of after-tax synergy value net of integration costs, against a £100m premium. Below the line, the deal transfers value to the seller.

canonical.q: Why do companies buy other companies?
canonical.a: Because they believe the target is worth more in their hands than the price they pay: cost synergies from duplicated functions, revenue synergies from cross-selling, a capability bought faster than it could be built, consolidation of a fragmented market, or cheap financing buying earnings. The premium only makes sense if the synergies that justify it are real and deliverable.

canonical.q: Is the deal accretive or dilutive?
canonical.a: Accretive if pro-forma EPS beats standalone EPS. The shortcut: compare the target's earnings yield at the offer price with the after-tax cost of the funding — the acquirer's own earnings yield for stock, the after-tax interest rate for debt or cash. Cash is usually cheapest, so all-cash deals are usually the most accretive. Accretion is arithmetic, not value creation.

Combined net income, less after-tax interest on new debt, less after-tax interest lost on cash spent, plus after-tax synergies, less any new amortisation from write-ups — that is pro-forma net income. Divide by the acquirer's shares plus the new shares issued (stock consideration over the acquirer's price). Compare with standalone EPS and state the percentage.

canonical.q: What is goodwill and where do synergies fit?
canonical.a: Goodwill is the residual: purchase price less the fair value of the target's identifiable net assets after write-ups. It sits on the balance sheet and is impairment-tested, not amortised. Synergies are the extra profit the combination earns — cost synergies are more credible than revenue ones because the buyer controls them — and their present value has to cover the premium for the deal to create value.

traps: Comparing P/Es at the market price. The test uses the P/E at the offer price — Tamar pays 12.5×, not Wychwood's 10× — and the after-tax cost of the funding actually used.
Adding the two net incomes and dividing by the old share count. The funding cost comes off the income and the new shares go into the denominator; forgetting either is the classic failure.
Charging pre-tax interest. Every funding cost — new debt, forgone interest on cash — enters the walk after tax.
Calling the premium goodwill. They are different numbers built on different bases: £100m over the market price, £220m over identifiable net assets.
Treating accretion as proof the deal is good. Overpaying with cheap debt is still accretive — the EPS line cannot see the NPV.
one_liners: A deal is accretive when the earnings you buy yield more, at the price you pay, than the after-tax cost of what you pay with.
